subtopic: REQUEST FOR REPORT ON PROPOSED CONFERENCE OF PROVINCES

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: REQUEST FOR REPORT ON PROPOSED CONFERENCE OF PROVINCES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, will the Prime Minister make a report to the house regarding the conference with the provincial premiers? He will recall that on May 10 last he stated this conference would take place in respect of constitutional matters. Will he also advise whether there is any prospect, on the basis of the consultations, that the provinces are now generally in support of the need for a bill of rights as part of a constitutional amendment rather than a statute only applicable to federal measures?

speakeroldname: Righi Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minisier):
subtopic: REQUEST FOR REPORT ON PROPOSED CONFERENCE OF PROVINCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, during our discussions yesterday afternoon, which occupied between two and three hours, the question of a conference to consider the direction of confederation and confederation problems was referred to by the premier of the province of Ontario, who indicated some months ago that he intended calling a conference for this purpose. Mr. Robarts made it clear that he had in mind a conference of provincial leaders, and that in his invitation to the provincial leaders he would indicate that he would invite the federal government to send observers. It was the consensus of the provincial leaders that if an invitation of this kind were issued, and it is likely that it will be sent shortly for a meeting in the fall, it would be accepted. If we receive such an invitation asking that a federal government observer be sent, we will be glad to send one.
The other matter mentioned by my right hon. friend was also of a constitutional nature, regarding the desirability of enshrining in our constitution a bill of rights which would have both federal and provincial application. I indicated to the provincial leaders that I would be sending an invitation in respect of a special federal-provincial conference to discuss this matter, to be held, I hope, either late in 1967 or early in 1968. The consensus was that a conference of this kind would be useful, and that the provinces would be glad to send representatives. I think we will be able to make progress on this very important aspect of constitutional development before many months have passed.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR REPORT ON PROPOSED CONFERENCE OF PROVINCES
speechtext:
Will the Prime Minister indicate that as a result of the discussions which took place there was any indication on the part of the two provinces which in 1959 and 1960 objected to constitutional amendments that they have changed their views? And in view of the fact that apparently the same objection to the convening of a conference on constitutional matters has been taken by these provinces, will he give further consideration to the suggestion that it would be generally desirable to attain unity, perhaps, by convening a constitutional conference in this centennial year? I suggest this because certainly the conference he has mentioned could not by any stretch of the imagination
July 6. 1967

Inquiries of the Ministry be successful so far as the whole spectrum of constitutional change or alteration is concerned.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR REPORT ON PROPOSED CONFERENCE OF PROVINCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the premier of Ontario, who first made the proposal for a constitutional meeting, himself indicated to us that this should not be considered as a constitutional conference in the sense that constitutional changes would be raised and discussed, but a conference to consider problems of confederation and the direction of confederation in a general way. It was felt that such a meeting would be a very useful and perhaps an essential preliminary to a later constitutional conference.
While a meeting of this kind is being held, with the federal government represented by observers, we are ourselves federally examining the problem through a special section of the Department of Justice, as has been announced to the house, and are developing our own ideas. This matter will subsequently be dealt with also in parliament. It is felt, and I think the heads of provincial governments would agree with this in view of the talk we had yesterday, that this is as far as we should go in the immediate future; that the conference in 1967 would not go beyond a general survey by the provincial leaders of our constitutional problems and the direction in which we are going as a confederation.

speechtext: I have a question, Mr. Speaker, which 1 should like to direct to the Minister of Trade and Commerce. Is it a fact that the United States import quota on Canadian Cheddar cheese has been raised, and if so by how much? speakeroldname: Hon. Robert Winters (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
maintopic: CHEESE-INCREASES IN QUOTAS ESTABLISHED BY UNITED STATES
speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Speaker, the quota has been raised. The United States administration, through Secretary Freeman, has now for the first time established a separate annual quota for aged Cheddar cheese with effect from July 1 last. This quota amounts to 1,225,000 pounds annually on a first come, first served basis and no import licences are required. Shipments to the United States under this quota would, however, have to be certified as being made from unpasteurized milk
[Mr. Laing.l
and aged not less than nine months. If Canadian producers are able to take up the whole of the quota this would represent a doubling of the 614,000 pound cheddar cheese quota previously available to Canada in the United States market.
In addition to this specific quota for aged cheddar, the United States administration have also substantially increased their overall quota for regular cheddar to 8.8 million pounds, as compared with the previous level of 2.8 million pounds. This quota for regular cheddar is not limited as to type of cheddar supplied. We are working with the United States authorities to ensure an appropriate portion of this over-all quota for Canada.

The hon. member for Calgary North asked about the increase in the dollar budget. I was asked how many airplanes we expected to get from the CF-5 program. At the moment the number is still 115, at a cost of $215 million. There is some possibility that we might alter the number of airplanes to a small extent, but if we did this we would expect a reduction in the cost of the program. In other words, under a $215 million program we should expect to get a total of 115 planes.
A question was raised with respect to the tankers to be provided for these airplanes. It has been decided it would not be advisable to use the Hercules. A question was also raised as to whether there will be sufficient pilots to man the CF-5's. I assure the committee that there is in fact no pilot shortage. There will be an adequate number of pilots to man these planes in the years ahead. They will come from the training stream, which is being augmented. In addition there will be some pilots available from the air division in Europe as the total contribution there diminishes. So we anticipate there will be enough pilots to meet the demands consequent upon the formation of these three new squadrons.

I wish to assure the house that on the basis of the most recent information given me by the commander of maritime command the manpower to run this vessel when it comes out of repair has been earmarked for many months. Supply-National Defence which could not be adequately determined until it was actually in refit. Mr. Chairman, the aim of the tactical satellite communications program is to develop satellite communications terminals and technology in tactical environments, that

is, aboard ship, in aircraft, and mobile terminals for the land forces. This is to be a joint NATO program, the governments participating being Belgium, Canada, Germany, Italy, the Netherlands, the United Kingdom and the sponsor, the United States. A draft memorandum of understanding has been prepared. It likely will be agreed to at a NATO meeting some time in the latter part of this summer and will then be presented to the participating countries for ratification shortly thereafter.
The United States has already launched the first experimental satellite. The participating countries have agreed to provide their own terminals and share the results of the test program. Canada has initiated procurement of two mobile terminals and will commence technical trials about December, 1967. The information thus acquired, and shared by all countries, will be used to develop tactical hardware in a later phase of the program. Canadian test terminals will be manned by Canadian military personnel already on establishment.
In so far as the relationship between this project and the possibility of Canada putting into orbit its own communications satellite is concerned, I am told there is no interference between the two projects.

Mr. Chairman, when these estimates were under discussion before I believe the minister mentioned there would be a second communications satellite to be shared by the United States, Australia and Canada. If I recall correctly from memory, there will be the possibility, under the program I have just discussed, of a second satellite being put in orbit at a later time in addition to the one the United States has already put into orbit. The question my hon. friend is asking has to do with the project known as project Mallard which is a trilateral project between the United States, Australia and Canada. So far as our capability to provide troops if they are needed in future is concerned, let me
July 6, 1967

Supply-National Defence say that we can meet any reasonable request. As my hon. friend knows, we have one battalion on stand-by which is instantly available for United Nations duties provided the government of Canada decides it is in the interest of this country to participate in some United Nations role. Whether or not the need would be for an infantry battalion, we do not know. Fundamental to the whole philosophy of United Nations peace keeping, it has been our experience, as related in the white paper, that no two requirements are alike. For that reason, rather than building up a special force we have found that we have been able to meet each requirement as it occurred. This is true because we have well trained and well equipped forces and are able to extract from them those men with the particular capability required at a particular time. I am sure this would again be true regardless of whether it was support personnel, an infantry battalion or something of that nature. It would be quite impossible to speculate as to the specific individuals, units or sub-units that would go until the actual requirement was known. I think my hon. friend will appreciate this.
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
So far as mobile command is concerned, its reorganization is coming along very successfully. This is a major reorganization, as my hon. friend knows, and it will take a number of years to implement it in full. In other words, it will take a number of years to acquire all the machinery and equipment that is required for the total force and to have the troops trained in the use of that equipment and bring them to the maximum of operational capability. Throughout this period they are maintaining their operational capability and enhancing it all the time, but I think it will reach a new peak of effectiveness in perhaps three or four years time, around 1970 or in the early 1970's.
It will take that long, because of the lead times involved, to acquire the equipment, make it available to the various formations, set up the training requirements for each of the equipments and train the troops to be proficient in their use. So I would think the present high capability would continue to rise throughout, say, this entire five year period but that it would reach a new peak of military effectiveness in four or five years time.

the Middle East developed very fast, a war started and it was over in six days. The United Nations is now having to consider at the diplomatic level all of the occurrences in the Middle East. This leads me to the question I wish to ask.

I may say that this expenditure is programmed to increase slightly in the years ahead. We will be providing more new equipment than has been provided in the immediate past. It does not mean we are going to provide new equipment for the total reserves as this is not feasible within our budgetary limitations, but it does mean we are going to provide sufficient up to date equipment to enable the men to see what the equipment looks like and when they exercise with the regular forces they will be in a position to make the maximum use of their training.

In the list that the minister gave us I noticed that no equipment was being provided for the army except for some communications equipment, and thus the minister's reluctance to give the type of breakdown that was asked for becomes more and more understandable. In addition to the point made by the hon. member for Vancouver East, that no equipment for the reserve forces was mentioned by the minister, no equipment was mentioned with reference to the army except for some communications equipment for what the minister now calls the land environment.
However, I should like to say something about the hydrofoil. I asked a number of questions with regard to the hydrofoil when the estimates were last discussed on June 22, and in reply a short time ago the minister merely said that the cost of this craft had been given in answer to written questions. Actually they were questions put on the order paper by the hon. member for Melville and they showed that the cost of
July 6. 1967

this program is now estimated at $50 million. I think this is a matter of very considerable concern to all members of the house. A great deal of consideration was given to the authorization of this program in 1961 and 1962. At that time the total cost of the program was supposed to be under $10 million. Now the cost has escalated to five times that amount and I think the end is not yet in sight. [DOT] (4:00 p.m.)
This seems to be an example of very poor estimating. I know there was a fire which caused some increase in costs, but it seems to me there must be some other reason for the enormous escalation in the cost of this program.
Looking at the Auditor General's report for 1966, we find that he goes into this matter in some detail. He indicates that in April, 1963, the estimated cost of the hydrofoil project was $9,100,000. Then, in March, 1964 it went up to $16,300,000. By June, 1964, only three or four months later, it was up to $20,655,000. By November of that year the cost had risen to $26 million. I should like to ask the minister the reason for this big jump in the estimated cost from $20 million to $26 million in the course of about six months. Then, in June 1965, another eight months or so later, the cost went up to $36 million, a jump of $10 million. By April, 1966, the cost had risen to $43 million. Now there is another big jump in the space of one year to $50 million.
What are the reasons for these very large increases in costs? As I say, in a few months' time the cost rose from $16 million to $20 million, from $26 million to $30 million and then from $43 million to $50 million. This is the type of thing which I believe causes a large number of people to lose confidence in estimates. We have an estimate for a certain amount of money for a certain project and then we find the cost has increased fivefold. Another example of an estimate which has increased by four or five times over the original estimate is the arts centre, close to where we are sitting. In view of our primary function as members of parliament to keep an eye on expenditures, I feel we should have a full explanation.

I agree with my hon. friend that the original estimate for this project was not as accurate as it might have been. Since my hon. friend was the minister at the time the original estimate was made, perhaps he could help me explain why the estimated cost was not more accurately forecast at that time. Since that time there have been a number of
Supply-National Defence contributing factors. There have been increases in taxes and wages. I presume, and I am saying this only from memory, that the weapons system has been included since I believe the anticipated cost of the weapons system is of the order of $10 million.
This figure was included in the amount the Minister of Defence Production gave the house yesterday. The total amount for the ship system, therefore, would be $40 million and about $10 million for the weapons system. In addition, there was the cost of the fire, as my hon. friend explained, the extended program period due to the fire and the extra overhead that is involved resulting from the extension of the program. My hon. friend is quite right, however, in pointing out one of the serious difficulties, particularly In development projects, of getting more accurate estimates. We are making an effort to improve the technique, and I feel with some success. I do not believe there will ever be perfection in this field because historically In this country, the United States, Great Britain and France, the estimated cost of these major development programs, airplane developments and ship developments, has escalated by a factor of two, three or four or even more over the original estimate.
Under our new system we are requiring much more extensive program definition than was the case previously. This in itself involves some expenditure. The aim of the project has to be more clearly outlined and the various steps involved recorded on paper. The cost of each of the steps involved has to be estimated with a greater degree of accuracy and detail than was previously undertaken. I fully expect this will reduce the margin of error in the future perhaps by 50 per cent, but I am not yet confident that any system has been devised which will predict accurately the cost of new development projects.
I should point out to my hon. friend, however, that as the cost increased the options available were to cancel it, which would have meant a total loss in so far as the determination of these new areas of knowledge is concerned which we were pursuing, or to continue to spend the extra money required and gain experience in a number of very important areas. This is a new method of propulsion. The fixed foil system for open ocean travel is a new concept. The method of transferring the power involved new techniques. The habitability of this kind of ship is unknown. For these and other reasons we felt that the knowledge which would be gained

Supply-National Defence for the armed forces through continuing the project and from taking the ship to sea for trials would justify the expense involved.

Dealing with the latter statement of the minister, I point out that when the project was first authorized it was, of course, on the basis of the high potential value it would have if it proved successful. It was authorized, to begin with, on the understanding that the cost was not going to run to anything like the figure it has. In other words, at that time the estimate was, as I understood it, practically guaranteed to be in the neighbourhood of $10 million. I should like to ask the minister if the contractors doing this work have been working on a fixed price contract or a cost plus contract, and to what extent has this contributed to the increase in the cost of this project?

I do not have the entire answer to this question, Mr. Chairman, since it relates to the responsibilities of the Minister of Defence Production. The original contract, which I think has been recently changed since the fire, involved a bonus incentive system whereby the units were priced out at agreed rates and there was an incentive to the contractor to try to complete the ship at less than the unit cost and in less than the prescribed time. If this were the case, his profit margin would have been enhanced. If it were not the case, he would suffer a loss.
It is very difficult with a development project of this kind to get a fixed price contract because there are so many unknown elements that no one would bid on it in those terms. However, I do not disagree with my hon. friend when he says that perhaps if the total cost had been anticipated at the time the project was authorized it might have been looked at differently. But when you get half way through a project and have spent $30 or $35 million, then the decision is really to spend another $15 million in order to gain knowledge in a number of areas that are of interest to you, and that is the decision you have to take and not the original one.

Has the supervision of this project been in the hands of the Defence Research Board, the naval construction branch of the department or who has been supervising the work being performed by the contractor?
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)

We have a project officer in the Department of National Defence in charge of the project, but of course the contract itself

is the responsibility of the Department of Defence Production and any increases in cost have to be approved by Treasury Board in the normal manner.
So far as recommendations to carry on with the project are concerned, this matter was considered at defence council where the advice of the chief of technical services and his officers, other senior staff officers and the defence research board was obtained. There was an opportunity for everyone who was interested to state their point of view before a decision was taken.

Mr. Chairman, I do not know that the minister quite understood the question. When a naval vessel is built-and this vessel is a naval vessel-there has always been to my knowledge a supervisory staff present at the site to ensure that the proper standards are met in constructing the vessel, in regard to the equipment put into it, and so on. Who is in charge of this on the construction of the hydrofoil?
Mr. Chairman, we have a naval captain in charge of the project who has officers responsible to him, and they are responsible for the technical standards.

Mr. Chairman, as a result of the fire that occurred on the hydrofoil the government and therefore the taxpayers have to spend an additional $3 million on the project. It is my understanding that the Department of National Defence has a project manager-I believe that is the term-present at all times. This gives rise to the question I have in mind. My information-and I would not disclose it unless I considered it authentic-is that the fire occurred because of the complete neglect of all safety factors at the shipyard. As I say, I have this information on what I consider the highest authority. Apparently there was inflammable material in the engine room at the time and when the engines were tested an explosion occurred followed by the fire.
I should like to ask the minister what report he has received from the project manager as to the cause of the fire and whether the cause was, as I am informed on highest authority, neglect of safety factors. If that was the case, then the $3 million extra cost should be a charge on the shipyard, not a charge on a department of the government or the taxpayers. Can the minister give the house any factual information from the report he received as to the cause of the fire and state whether or not there was complete neglect of safety factors in construction?

Mr. Chairman, there was a board of inquiry and I would not want to answer the question without getting a copy of its report and refreshing my memory. I do not think the situation was as my hon. friend states. Certainly that is not my recollection of it, but I would not want to comment without taking another look at the findings of the board.

Mr. Chairman, I am also interested in the answer given by the minister in regard to the assumed total cost of the hydrofoil project. It was rather significant that in this morning's paper there appeared another item dealing with defence but in relation to another country altogether. It tells of the decision of France to pull out of a joint venture with the British to build an Anglo-French V-G aircraft, which was to be a very sophisticated strike and reconnaissance aircraft. It was hoped that it would be the pride of the Royal Air Force after delivery in 1975, but the scheme has been shot down.
The last two paragraphs of the article have some interesting things to say about the experimental work that goes on in the defence industry and I think it applies equally to Canada in relation to the hydrofoil project. The article has this to say:
Industrially, the V-G was considered vital because it gave Britain's substantial aircraft industry a chance to work on a technically advanced model. The theory was that such work would produce valuable expertise for British industry as a spin-off.
Without advanced military projects, British airframe makers may be unable to keep first-class designers on their payrolls. The industry would decline, it is feared, and dependence on U.S. planes would increase.
It seems to me, Mr. Chairman, looking at the estimates of the department and noting the enormous expenditure on defence by a country with the population of Canada, that we should seriously question whether in this day and age we should be prepared to launch into experimental work in defence unless it is almost guaranteed that there will be some valuable spin-off into private industry of some commercial worth as a result. I also feel we need to pause and reflect on the fact that our dependence on the United States for defence, as the dependence of Britain or any other country which associates itself with the western group of nations, will be increasingly greater. I noticed that the minister of external affairs was with us for a while this afternoon listening to this debate, and I regret that he has now left because external affairs and foreign policy are so keenly involved here.
Supply-National Defence
The real question for Canadians now is not what we spend on defence or what kind of projects we will launch or are launching but rather whose umbrella we are under. I asked a question during the question period today which related very indirectly to which side we were on in today's world. A related question dealing with a matter outside the minister's department was asked by the hon. member for Grey-Bruce on June 19. It concerned the training of pilots for Algeria under external aid. The Prime Minister promised at that time that an answer would be given the next day. I looked at the next day's Hansard but did not find an answer there, and I have not had time to make a diligent search to see whether an answer was given.
On that occasion the Leader of the Opposition asked: When did they become our allies? I know that the official opposition has been very preoccupied lately with its own labyrinth of leadership problems and in various ways has been marching along roads more tangled, I am sure, than the streets of the Casbah, but I can tell the Leader of the Opposition when Algeria became an ally of ours. It was in March, 1966, a day or two prior to March 18; I cannot be exact on the date. We then signed an accord with that nation which involved providing a variety of forms of aid, and if the information presented by the hon. member for Grey-Bruce is the case, something very close to military aid was to be provided and so is very important to us today.
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
It seems to me that we do not examine closely at the present time who our allies are, where our aid is going and for what purposes it is given. Though we spend $1,688 million on defence we seem to be engaged in several external affairs policies that could be detrimental to the very defence that we boast we are spending so much for.
The minister mentioned the hydrofoil program. I wonder what other experimental programs we are engaged in at the present time. Much could be learned from this program and the way that its costs have accelerated. I doubt that there will be much spin-off into private industry or into the shipbuilding industry of Canada from this project. It seems to me that at a much earlier time we might have shown the sort of realism that France has shown with some of its defence projects. We might have cut this project off. It was not a joint project but entirely our own.

Supply-National Defence
Incidentally, defence costs in future will be such that there could be increasing collaboration between Canada and other middle powers and small, industrialized countries on a variety of ventures. Here again, when becoming involved in joint defence projects with other countries of the world we shall need to be extremely concerned about who our allies are and when and why they have become our allies.
It behooves all members in the opposition to be aware of small matters which go unnoticed. Our cultural agreement with Algeria, our exchange agreement with that country, went unnoticed because it was alluded to only in the French language press of this country. The English language press did not mention it. The agreements aroused little interest when they were entered into.
We are involved in a complicated scheme which goes by the name of Francophonie. This scheme is motivated by the highest cultural motives, the aims of which are to increase exchanges between countries that use the French language. Several nations of North Africa, particularly because of their histories, are involved in the use of this language. We tend to enter into agreements with those countries despite their being governed by regimes that ordinarily we would not countenance. Through the highest of motives we enter into alliances that will come home to roost in ways we least expect. The hon. member for Grey-Bruce mentioned one such matter which came into prominence with the outbreak of war in the Middle East. That war caught us by surprise, and policies such as contributing to a United Nations peace keeping force, policies in which we had put our trust, were found to be incapable of fulfilling the purposes for which they had been designed.
As we reach the point where we end discussion of defence estimates we should think carefully of the total costs involved in expenditures for external affairs and defence matters. We should be prepared to examine and to rethink schemes such as the hydrofoil project. We should think carefully about what we are doing in both these fields of government activity.
I appreciate the close questioning that the hon. member for Calgary North has directed toward the hydrofoil scheme, because its total cost of $50,006,000, is staggering, especially if one thinks of 50 $1 million schools or 50 $1 million hospitals. An equivalent sum could have been spent in a variety of constructive ways in Canada.

The minister has expressed the wish that the added knowledge the military personnel will gain will prove worth while. If that added knowledge is confined only to the armed forces it will be worth no more than the worth of a new toy. Such knowledge, in return for an expenditure of $50 million, will not increase the defence capability of Canada. I hope it may be possible to translate some of that knowledge into the private industrial, productive, and commercial sector of this country.

Mr. Chairman, as I rise to speak there are two main questions I wish to ask about this department. I will not refer to details. The first question is: In view of what has happened since we had the opportunity to question the minister in February, March and April of this year and in view of what happened in the Middle East recently, what is to be the future role of the armed forces of Canada? My second question is: Is there a role for Canadian peace keeping forces in the world today? Before the minister enunciates defence policy I would ask him to answer these two questions.
For a few moments I wish to refer to some comments the minister made in opening the discussion of his estimates. As found on page 1816 of Hansard for June 22 he said:
The purpose of our defence policy is not and never was to create simply a giant peace keeping force.
That is a far cry from what he said in this house several months ago. The minister shakes his head. I shall quote certain statements he made before the defence committee. I take it from the minister's nod at the present time that he is indicating that he never maintained that one of the purposes of his defence policy was to create a giant peace keeping force.
I always said it was one of the purposes but not the sole purpose. So long as my hon. friend clearly delineates this distinction I am sure that we shall both be on common ground.

Yes. That is what I want to get straight, Mr. Chairman. I find it hard to reconcile what the minister said on the defence estimates previously and what he has said at the present time with some statements that the chief of the general staff has made. The hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre referred to those statements. I ask the minister whether the chief of the general staff had
July 6. 1967

authority to make the statement which is attributed to him in the Globe and Mail o f April 24. The hon. member tor Winnipeg South Centre referred to that article which is headed, "Mobile Peace Force Is Goal." Then follow the general's remarks:
The creation of a mobile world peace keeping force as well as elimination of waste are the goals of Canada's proposed reorganization-
The minister a few moments ago said that this is not one of the goals of defence policy. Whom are the people of Canada to believe? Are they to believe the chief of general staff or the Minister of National Defence? Is this another red herring with which the minister is trying to confuse the public? Regardless of the question asked him, he can say both yes and no to it. I will refresh the minister's memory as to what the chief of the general staff has said. He has told us that Canada's forces are being made into a highly mobile force in keeping with their role as peace keepers in the world. He further said that in the wake of the defence white paper it was clear that Canada was committed diplomatically and militarily to an expanding peace keeping role. Here again, I say that the statements of the chief of staff are not in accord with what the minister has just told us. This is one of the matters we should clear up before we go further with these estimates. Just what is Canada's defence policy? Let the minister get up and express it clearly. I invite him to do so in the course of this debate. This is the time.
[DOT] (4:30 p.m.)

Yes, the policy is as stated in the white paper of 1964 and as reiterated by the Secretary of State for External Affairs in this house a few weeks ago and by myself. The priorities are set out at page 24 of the white paper on defence and they are still in effect.

Some of us believe the emphasis has been placed on peace keeping. The minister informed us in the committee in no uncertain terms that this was the major role. The subject was discussed many times in the committee. We were afraid we might be opting out of our collective commitments under NATO and NORAD, though the minister denied this when it was brought to his attention during the latter part of the debate.
Some people think Canada is taking a position of neutrality in her approach to external affairs. If this is the case all the figures we are referring to today might very well be wiped out. Before Canada adopts a position of
Supply-National Defence neutrality we should reflect upon what happened to certain other countries which adopted a similar attitude. I say that Canada cannot possibly take such a position because of her geographical situation. If a neutral country lies in the path of an aggressor the aggressor will not recognize a declaration of neutrality. Think of what happened to Belgium and Holland in the first world war. Canada cannot adopt a neutral role in world affairs today. We are committed to the collective defence of our country and this, I think, is the major consideration in any policy devised for our protection. We must honour our commitments for peace in the world.
The minister also told us that during the period of reorganization there had been no falling off in our organizational capacity but that on the contrary in practically every field our operational capacity had been enhanced. I wonder what basis the hon. gentleman had for making such a statement. Is this his opinion or is it the opinion of our allies? I understand that under the program of reorganization which the minister has undertaken, the force for which his department is responsible, will no longer fit in with the requirements of NATO commanders. Maybe the minister is putting the cart before the horse. We are devising a force unlike any force in the world and then expecting NATO and allied commanders to use it. The first step should be to ascertain what the requirements of these various forces are likely to be and the best way in which our forces can fit into the general scheme as devised by NATO commanders.
I submit too that in attempting to insist upon Canada's idea that there should be a peace keeping force we are also putting the cart before the horse. It has been obvious for many years in the history of the United Nations that many of the great powers in that organization do not want a peace keeping force. The minister stated as much during his opening remarks in this debate. He said that certain factors, economic, political and so on, should be decided first. I agree, and if these factors were correctly dealt with there might be no need for a peace keeping force at all. I cannot for the life of me see why Canada should be so insistent upon putting a peace keeping force into areas where such a force is not wanted and not required.
The minister mentioned this himself when he was referring to the supervisory organization in Palestine. He said it was possible that the United Nations might have to build on that organization to supply a United Nations
July 6, 1967

Supply-National Defence presence in the Middle East as a result of recent developments. I would ask the minister this question. As a result of the recent developments in the Middle East, does he think that while we are here as members of this parliament any of the countries of the Middle East will ever ask Canada to participate in a peace keeping force in that area? I doubt it very much. It may be unjust to say that this is the result of statements made by some members of the present cabinet, but I doubt that the Arabs would ever ask Canada to participate in any peace keeping force.
What good is accomplished by sending such a force to that area? The minister tells us it kept the peace for ten years. I do not believe that. I think the Israelis and the Arabs kept the peace themselves. I And fault with the United Nations for failing to make some effort to solve the economic and political problems which existed in the region. The very fact that the refugees were there for so many years, neglected by the United Nations, is one of the factors which contributed to the recent outbreak. I believe Canada should put forward more effort in the debates at the United Nations in calling attention to the necessity of eliminating these problems rather than spending Canadian money on once more establishing a force which is not required and which to my mind was of very little use during the ten years in which it served in the Gaza Strip.
The minister said that the fault was not with the peace keeping force but with the failure to come to grips with the social, economic and political problems which made the peace keeping force necessary in the first place. He was referring to the withdrawal of the UNEF force from the Gaza strip. He went on to say it was typical of the efficiency of this force and of transport command that when the word came to leave the area the force was removed in a remarkably effective manner. I fail to see how the minister or any Canadian can take pride in what happened to our force at that time. I wonder, though, whether this is what the minister had in mind when in January of this year he told us that Canada will have her name indelibly etched as a world leader in military organization. Or is this what he meant when he made the statement that Canadians were now becoming leaders in defence organization, not just followers? Just what did he mean? In this respect the hon. gentleman said:
In this regard I would like to emphasize the success, not failure, of our Canadian soldiers and


airmen of our force in Gaza. To keep the peace in such an area for more than ten years was a remarkable achievement for the force which included more than 10,000 Canadian soldiers and airmen who served there since the inception of the operation. They should all be proud of their accomplishment.
I suggest that they actually did nothing during the ten years they were there. When the Arabs and the Israelis no longer wanted them there they told the Secretary General of the United Nations to take them out and they were taken out. How can one give the Canadian force credit for keeping the peace in the area in those circumstances? They certainly did not.
[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)
I think that again we are putting the cart before the horse. I think we should concentrate our efforts in the United Nations on an attempt to overcome the problems which we know exist. I believe Canadian funds are being wasted. The same thing is apparently happening in Cyprus.
I say to the minister that with the addition of the peace restoring role he is getting deeper and deeper into hot water than he has been. It is a more dangerous role. The fact that we have so few troops means that we cannot be an effective force in that regard in any event. During the debate in the defence committee I believe figures were presented concerning how many personnel would be needed to keep a force of 1,000 men in the field in such a role. The minister is aware that any time Canada has sent forces overseas she has relied on other nations to look after their supply.
If the minister says, as he said a few moments ago, that it is not the intention to concentrate on peace keeping, then why did he put all the emphasis on mobility and the ability to supply these forces when he talked to us in February, March and April of this year. At this time I should like to ask the minister to clarify, for me at least, what he meant by his statement in respect of peace keeping and to explain how he can reconcile it with what the chief of the general staff has said. Is the minister right or is the chief of the general staff right? I think Canadians are entitled to know this. I should like the minister to reply to this before I ask any further questions.

He has been given the opportunity to answer this question. I think the Canadian people have a right to an answer of some kind. I do not want to repeat what the chief of the general staff as said. He did say, however, that peace keeping is the goal of present government defence policy. Is he right and has he the authority to speak for the department? If not, he should shut up and I think the minister should tell him to. If the minister permits the chief of the general staff to make this kind of speech, then surely he should get up in the house and support what the general has said or deny it. I believe the minister owes the people of Canada an answer in this regard.

No. We are being faced this afternoon with the typical reaction of the Minister of National Defence. For four years he has stubbornly refused to disclose facts and give information to members of the house. It is to be expected that we would be a trifle annoyed at this. We have had four long years under this stubborn and obstinate Minister of National Defence during which time he has concealed information from us, has sat silent and has refused to answer questions. He did not give a satisfactory answer this afternoon to the question with regard to equipment for our forces. He has not given an answer to the member who has just spoken. He has not answered the things which were said when we discussed the estimates on June 22. We have had silent treatment and evasive answers from the minister.
Some time ago I asked the minister about our naval commitments this summer with regard to NATO. He did not have the information then and he has not given it since. Is he prepared to give it now? What are our naval forces doing, if anything, with regard to NATO this summer? We get nothing from the minister except great statements about how wonderful his program is and that he is striking out on a new departure which will be an example to the world. These statements are not based on fact; they are not supported by evidence. I have just read a very interesting book by a member of the cabinet in England who resigned last year. I forget his exact position but I believe he was associated with the minister of national defence. This gentleman was here in 1965 at which time he looked into the matter of the rearrangement of Canada's defence forces. With the minister and his officials he examined the program of

Supply-National Defence unification. In his book he sets out very clearly that he believes such a program would be unsuitable for the United Kingdom to follow. He says that it sounds fine to have a unified force with everybody in one uniform and everybody put together but that in actual fact it will not work. So he rejected it and the minister of national defence in England rejected it.
The other day I spoke to a member of the Australian parliament. I told him that during the course of a defence debate we had here our minister used as evidence the example of a civil servant in Australia who had written an article commending the project of unification. I asked him whether he knew anything about this. He said he had never heard of it before. Yet the minister paraded that in the house as evidence that other countries are keenly interested in what we are doing and are about to follow suit. All these years have gone by and no other country in the world has followed the course laid out by the minister. As I have said time and time again the people of this country have been confused and bemused by the minister's statements. The minister has no good evidence to give us.
Earlier this afternoon the minister was asked about the mobile force. He now tells us that it will take four to five years to get it in shape for action. Yet he has fed us propaganda to the effect that this mobile force would be ready on almost instant notice to go anywhere in the world and play a part. Now he says that it will take four to five years. All he could tell us this afternoon is that one battalion is ready for service on the request of the United Nations.
This is a very confusing picture indeed. The minister has been asked questions about the role at which Canada is aiming. We spoke about this at some length on June 22. No answer has been given. We heard again the statement made by the chief of the defence staff to the effect that this is the major role for Canada. He said that the transformation-that is the word which was used by the chief of the general staff when he appeared before the committee-set out in the white paper was to alter our role to one of peace keeping under United Nations auspices. The minister has made no reply to this. Obviously he agrees with the chief of the general staff. Perhaps he told him to make the statement as a roundabout way of attempting to influence the public.
The minister is now saddled with a failure in his much lauded cost efficiency or cost

Supply-National Defence accounting procedure. I recall many occasions when he accused our government of failing to estimate costs correctly. With great glee he used the example of the armoured personnel carrier. Now he has a hydrofoil on his hands. The cost of this project is about four times as great as it was estimated it would be and it is not finished. Yet this minister has told us that he has set up a system which is so superior that this type of error would not occur.
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
The minister criticized the hon. member for Calgary North about the difficulties he encountered in respect of the armoured personnel carrier. Now he has his own white elephant, the hydrofoil, and he does not know what to do with it. He has talked about efficiency and a new method of determining expenditures and costs, but what has he saddled us with at this time? He has created enormous expenditures amounting to millions of dollars but has given no satisfactory explanation as to the progress or effectiveness of this project. He has given no explanation why other countries appear to have had greater success with a similar type of vessel. He is afraid to cancel the program. Instead he carries it on, perhaps in order to load it on his successor after he leaves the Department of National Defence this year. At that time I suppose he hopes to be free of complaints.
The record of the minister over the last four years is one of colossal failure and the people of Canada are beginning to realize it. His unification of the forces has proved to be ineffective and unwise, and the people of Canada clearly realize now that the wiping out of the history and traditions of our fighting men was an unsatisfactory step.
During the last week the people have been able to observe our forces, particularly the army, in their special regimental uniforms, proudly displaying their esprit de corps. I bring this matter to the attention of the house because I believe that a gross and grave injustice is being done to this man. The royal prerogative permits the crown, even today, to deny the individual the right to know the reasons why action is taken against him. That principle, which over the years has been basic to the system of constitutional monarchy, is no longer applicable. In 1953 or 1954, I think it was, the high court of the United Kingdom decided that no individual could be deprived of his rights by the simple

All of us remember the story of Archer-Shee. In the United Kingdom in 1911 Arch-er-Shee was fired from the naval college he was attending. The reason given was that he had been guilty of wrongdoing. The most able counsel in Britain at that time, Sir Edward Carson, undertook that case and fought it for several years against an almost impenetrable stand taken by the military authorities. Finally Archer-Shee was cleared. One of the first officers of the Old Contemptibles in the expeditionary force in 1914 to fall in France was Lieutenant Archer-Shee. Mr. Chairman, just before the supper adjournment the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway raised a question regarding the attachment of pay, allowances and pensions for alimony purposes. According to the Queen's Regulations and Orders, article 207.02(2):
When there is in effect an order or decree enforceable under the laws of Canada or any province thereof requiring payment to be made by an officer or man in respect of the support, care or maintenance of his wife or former wife or any legitimate or illegitimate child, the commanding officer may order a monthly compulsory allotment of pay as prescribed in (3) of this article.
[The Chairman.]
Section (3) of this article states:
The compulsory pay allotment shall consist of such portion of the pay of the officer or man, not exceeding the amount of the order or decree, as the commanding officer from time to time thinks fit, but no such compulsory pay allotment shall, in any month, exceed an amount equal to ten days pay of the officer or man.
So an active service officer or man can be required to support his dependants. Further this article states in section (9):
When there is no order or decree in effect but it has been represented to the Chief of the Defence Staff that an officer or man has deserted or is otherwise without reasonable cause failing to maintain his wife or any child under the age of 16, the Chief of the Defence Staff may order deductions to be made from the pay of the officer or man in the manner and subject to the limits prescribed in (2) and (3) of this article.
With respect to those officers on pension, the hon. lady will find in section 14, appendix 22, of the Canadian Forces Superannuation Act-and I am quoting subsection (2)-the following:
Where any court in Canada of competent jurisdiction has made an order requiring a recipient to pay an amount to his spouse, former spouse, child or other dependant and the court has issued to the minister a notice, in the form prescribed by the regulations, requesting on behalf of the recipient that there be paid to the person named in the order an amount specified in the notice, the amount so specified or any lesser amount specified by the minister shall, if the minister so directs, be deducted either in a lump sum or in instalments from any amount that is or is about to become payable to the recipient under this act, and shall be paid to the person named in the order.
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, it appears that in both these cases, if a court order is obtained it would be applied within the regulations and orders of the Canadian Armed Forces. In the case of diversion of pension under the Canadian Forces Superannuation Act, it is the current policy not to divert more than 50 per cent. Under the Defence Services Pension Continuation Act a court order is not necessary. The matter is investigated by the Department of Veterans Affairs and the minister acts on their recommendation.
Finally I should like to deal with the question that the Judge Advocate General's department provides legal help for the Canadian Armed Forces. I am informed by the Judge Advocate General that the Judge Advocate General simply informs the serviceman of the legal implications of any order but does not appear in court on the serviceman's behalf. If I may be permitted to create a pun, the legal officers of the Judge Advocate General's department advise the serviceman to get a lawyer. I think this answer should satisfy the concern expressed by the hon. lady.

speechtext:
I should like to ask the minister a few questions having to do with the disposal of property owned by the Department of National Defence on the west coast. However,

Supply-National Defence first I would like to compliment him, in view of the criticism which he has received today from the other side of the house, on the businesslike way in which he has been running his department. Over the last five years our national income has risen from roughly $40 billion to $60 billion. In other words it has gone up 50 per cent. We have seen expenditures on many fronts go up by comparable amounts. On the other hand, the expenditures of the Department of National Defence have been kept constant. Five years ago they were $1.7 billion a year, that is for the year 196364, and this year 1967-68, they are estimated to be the same amount, that is $1.7 billion.
But what is the size of our forces?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
In other words, our outlay on defence as a percentage of the national income has gone down from more than 4 per cent in 1963 to about 3 per cent in 1967. Considerable evidence meanwhile has been presented both in the house and in the committees of the house, that the effectiveness of our armed forces has been substantially increased. So I would say that for the same number of dollars-dollars with a declining purchasing value-to get a greater value in terms of defence in this country is no mean accomplishment.
I would like to deal more specifically with property owned by the Department of National Defence and then say a word about the disposal of lands which have been acquired by the department over the years. I understand that under the present minister a new policy was instituted. It was instituted a few years ago and it gave a real incentive to the members of the armed forces with authority over supply to get rid of surplus supplies, to sell off land that the Department of National Defence no longer required, and to dispose of inventories, out-dated materiel, ammunition, equipment, etc.
The policy was that the Department of National Defence would itself receive and keep the funds which resulted from selling off these surplus properties. In other words, the officers responsible for the administration and disposal of surplus materials, land and so on, could count on having this money put back into the coffers of the defence department and not paid over to the Receiver General of Canada.
This was a revolutionary idea because prior to that time there was no real incentive for the defence department, particularly for
2332	COMMONS
Supply-National Defence those in the armed forces, to dispose of land, equipment etc., they merely accumulated and maintained them, guarded them and watched them deteriorate. In the last few years we have seen the disposal of a substantial amount of property which was deteriorating, and which otherwise would have deteriorated to no value whatsoever.
In my own particular riding there was a large ordnance depot. I would put its present value at around $3 million. It was built in 1944 for naval stores and it continued to be filled with the same naval stores as were put into it in 1945. When the present minister took over in 1963 it was like a naval museum with guards but no one was allowed to see it. This materiel it contained was promptly disposed of under the new policy. It was turned over to the Crown Assets Disposal Corporation, and subsequently sold to the National Harbours Board. This property, on the waterfront in Vancouver, is now earning an income of the order of $300,000 a year. So instead of being a liability, it is a source of revenue to the people of Canada. This is the kind of policy, the kind of businesslike thinking and the kind of management which we need not only in our private affairs but also in the affairs of the government.
There are one or two other properties in my riding which I would like to see disposed of, one of them being a rifle range. It is located on 500 acres which used to be a long way out in the bush. Subsequently a $20 million bridge was built across the Vancouver harbour, almost to the doorstep of this property. These 500 acres suddenly became extremely valuable.
Is the hon. member referring to the Blair rifle range?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
Yes, the Blair rifle range in north Vancouver. Residential properties of considerable value are building up around this range. Roughly a third of the Blair range land has been cleared. Occasionally the clearing is used as a rifle range, but the rest is still covered with trees. I urge that the Department of National Defence turn all of this property over to the Crown Assets Disposal Corporation, in effect sell it to the highest bidder, and with part of the proceeds buy other land farther away and develop a comparable rifle range, if one is required.
I have corresponded with the defence department concerning this matter. I was told it is prepared to consider this proposal and that shortly it will be sending out one of its appraisers to look at this land with a

DEBATES	July 6, 1967
view to selling it for residential purposes. The district of north Vancouver has already zoned this property. It is an ideal property for residential construction. My own estimate of the value of these 500 acres is $3,000 an acre, so that it should be worth at least $1 million. The national defence department would have at least $1 million in hand with which, I am sure, they could buy several other rifle ranges. Let us hope they can get one other rifle range with a fraction of that money, put the rest back in the kitty-thus reducing the sum total of new taxation required to pay our defence bill.
I should like to speak now about another property which is a classic case. It is on Jericho beach in the Vancouver area occupied by the Department of National Defence. Jericho Beach is on the north side of Point Grey and forms part of the outer harbour in Vancouver. It is one of the finest recreational areas in Canada, located near an area referred to as Spanish Banks, where early Spanish explorers first dropped anchor. They dropped anchor there because it was an ideal location. There are miles and miles of sandy beach there. When the tide goes out, the beach runs out half a mile. It looks across at the coast range, which is snow capped, and into the downtown area of Vancouver. It is a beautiful spot. Yet, right in the centre of that long beach there is a defence base. The defence base is located there because originally it was a seaplane base. During world war II the Department of National Defence bought out a handsome golf course and several expensive homes in that area. They bought approximately 154 acres. Ever since the beginning of world war II there has been a defence base bisecting the beach there, requiring everyone travelling along Marine drive in Vancouver to circumvent this area of 154 acres. What is there now? The golf course went to rack and ruin. Gigantic hangars were built in the early 1940's and paint is now peeling off them. There are only a few hundred men in uniform there now. According to a recent editorial in one of the Vancouver papers, the area is now being used as a supply depot by the construction engineers detachment, transportation section, supply section, and maintenance subsection. Basically this is a supply depot for the army base at Chilliwack which is approximately 100 miles away.
[DOT] (8:20 p.m.)
This waterfront land is extremely valuable. It is land which politician after politician,

They all require training facilities. I plead with the minister through you, Mr. Chairman, not to sell it for a million dollars; it is worth a lot more than that. Do not sell it until proper arrangements have been made for training facilities right from rifles through submachine guns to light machine guns and three-inch mortars. There is no purpose served by trying to train a person in an armoury in the use of these weapons. You must have an actual firing range in the immediate area.
Now, that is all I am going to say about the Blair range. I want to thank the hon. member for what he had to say. I just want to add this, sir, because it is my home. There is only one block which prevents a complete beach area from Spanish Banks to Jericho, around Kit-silano, around False Creek, English Bay, First, Second and Third Beaches, around

Supply-National Defence Stanley Park until you hit Coal Harbour entrance. This is a most fantastic area with only one block, the Jericho Beach area, preventing a complete waterfront drive. Two very brief comments, Mr. Chairman. The first relates to national defence headquarters. The development of the new national defence headquarters should take place as quickly as possible. The second matter about which I want to comment is the thrill that so many people experienced on seeing the display yesterday on parliament hill. It was a wonderful show, with Her Majesty the Queen and all the colour of the uniforms there. This indicates to us that within our human hearts there is

something that has an appeal that is not going to be satisfied by a simple green uniform.

Mr. Chairman, I think I should reply at once to those two suggestions, and I should like to deal with the second one first. Mr. Chairman, I do not know whether this is the right vote under which to raise the matter I have in mind. This is a department that over the last five years has spent about $85 million per year in buying equipment, material and supplies. I realize that the department keeps a physical inventory of this equipment, but if any member of parliament should ask the Minister of National Defence to give him the value of this inventory, that is, the cost price of the inventory, the minister could not answer. The department is not keeping a dollar value of its inventory. It is only keeping a record of the physical count. This is no way to run a business. It is obsolete, it is old fashioned, and it is not good housekeeping.
To improve the situation would involve only a matter of tabulating when the equipment was bought, counting it and recording the cost price of the equipment. This record would become very valuable when the Department of National Defence turns its obsolete equipment over to Crown Assets for sale to the public. Goodness knows, the department turns over a great deal of equipment to Crown Assets because the equipment has become obsolete. If we ask Crown Assets
July 6, 1967

what this equipment cost, they cannot tell us because the Department of National Defence cannot tell them.
I ask the minister: Are you endeavouring to keep not only a physical inventory but a record of the dollar value of the inventory; and if so, at what stage is the department, and does the minister hope to have this system in operation in the near future?

The answer is yes, Mr. Chairman, the previous system, which we all felt to be inadequate, is being changed. We have it practically up to date at the present time and by this time next year it should be thoroughly accurate in so far as inventories are concerned, and broken down by activity within the department. We are at the moment, I think for the first time in living memory, in the process of calculating a dollar inventory value based upon cost.
It is high time.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on June 21 I asked the Registrar General whether he could indicate why the price of a ten pound bag of sugar in Canada's third largest city, Vancouver, had risen from 97 cents at the beginning of June to $1.12 at the present time. In view of the fact that within the last half hour this evening we have passed, if my arithmetic is correct, the sum of $3,416,295,507.08, it seems to me slightly bewildering to think we should be concerning ourselves about this rise in the price of sugar. It is bewildering until one realizes that for people across the country the costs of sugar, bread, meat and milk are the costs that matter most, and some of our people unfortunately have smaller means than they should have with which to meet these costs.
[DOT] (10:00 p.m.)
I want to stress that the price of sugar in Vancouver within a three-week period rose from 95 cents to $1.12. The public was given no reason for that increase. One correspondent of mine in Vancouver was told by a merchant that the Israeli-Arab war caused the price increase. She said that that could not have been correct as sugar stocks were on hand before the war broke out. The war could not have affected sugar prices in so short a period.
I also wish to emphasize that on June 17 Christie's Bread announced that it would increase the price of its 24 ounce loaf to retailers by two cents, and the one pound loaf to retailers by one cent, effective as of June 26. Shoppers in Ontario and Quebec are affected by this increase. Also, on June 23 General Bakeries Limited and Canada Bread Company raised their prices. General Bakeries Limited raised its prices by the amount that Christie's had raised theirs, and Canada
July 6, 1967	COMMONS
Bread Company increased its price for the 24 ounce loaf by one cent.
Though the Registrar General is new to his job it is high time that he looked into matters affecting consumers. On June 16, in the speech in which he outlined his plans for the whole department under his control, he said, as reported on page 1608 of Hansard:
It is all very well to go off in all directions like a chicken with its head off, but I feel this would only cause unnecessary distortions in marketing practices and would provoke more difficulties than it would solve. If I were to suggest something which perhaps is un-Canadian, I might say I think we should have facts before we have policy. I intend to proceed with all deliberate speed in that fashion.
I am afraid that Canadian consumers will get the idea, if they have not already got it, that the minister is proceeding with more deliberation than speed, when one considers the price increases of commodities such as sugar and bread that I have spoken of tonight. The cost of living index is steadily creeping upward and has done so for items such as rent, household appliances, as well as many other commodities which are taken into account in the cost of living index.
I appreciate that the minister cannot single handed investigate what is happening. He cannot run to the bakeries to ask why prices are going up; nor can he go to sugar refineries to ask why their prices are rising. I believe that there should be a board-some of us have called it a prices review board-to look into price increases and to determine whether they are justified by increased costs that manufacturers have to pay.
I notice that when the prices of bread charged by Christie's were increased, H. A. Vivian, vice president of sales for Christie's Bread division of National Biscuit Company of New York, refused to say what the price increase is to retailers. He did not want the public to know what the dealer margin is. The joint committee of the Senate and House of Commons on prices feels that that is exactly what the consumer should know. I urge the minister to establish within his department at once a fact finding body to determine why prices are going up.
The consumers are being most patient. The costs of bread, milk, sugar, housing and rents have increased, raising the cost of living. The price of milk has increased recently, as has the price of sugar. The cost of housing and of medical services has risen, together with many other items which make up the cost of living. Increasingly consumers will want to

If the minister knows, let him tell us tonight why the cost of sugar increased in Vancouver. That is a specific inquiry I have to make. If he can do so, let him also tell us why there have been increases in the prices of bread and milk-increases which have caused great concern to families across this country. If the hon. gentleman does not know the reason, I should like him to tell us what steps he will take to ascertain it under his fine program of finding out the facts before making policy.

wish to say to the hon. lady in reply to the specific question she asked that Canadian refined sugar prices react almost immediately to changes in the world price for raw sugar. As a result of the Middle East crisis, world raw sugar prices advanced in early June and prices for refined sugar went up accordingly. Thus the B.C. Sugar Refinery in Vancouver, which was selling 100 lbs of cane sugar on June 1 for $7.85 had by June 5 raised its price to $8.95 per 100 lbs. Between June 5 and June 20 four reductions in price were made and by June 20 the refinery price was down to $7.40 per 100 lbs, lower than it had been on June 5. Similar price changes were made by the refiners in eastern Canada. It is to be hoped that retail prices will soon reflect the decreases in refinery prices which have taken place since June 5, if they have not already done so.
On the general question of prices, I wish to say to the hon. lady that constitutionally neither the federal government nor parliament has the authority to impose pervasive controls over the price of goods and services, except in a national emergency such as war. Consequently parliament would not have the authority to enact legislation regulating prices.
The movement of prices depends on a number of complicated factors. Some of the factors depend on world economic conditions; others relate to domestic fiscal, monetary and tariff policy. The conditions and economic expectations of the marketplace also come into play.
Under the Combines Investigation Act it is the responsibility of the Director of Investigation and Research to scrutinize all significant price movements which come to his attention and which may involve illegal restraints on competition. He is charged under that statute with the duty of initiating an

It costs a Canadian homebuyer $840 more today than it did yesterday for a house financed under a government-insured mortgage of $18,000 over 25 years.
The hike-$33.60 a year-came within a whisker of being twice that much.
Costs are up because Central Mortgage and Housing Corp. last night boosted the National Housing Act interest rate from 7 to 7i per cent.
I would imagine the reason this was done was that the minister thought there would be an increase in housing.
Here are some of the comments which are pertinent to this increase:
A C.M.H.C. official in Ottawa said the increase would "hopefully" make N.H.A. mortgages attractive enough to stimulate lending-and building.
However, John McCulloch, C.M.H.C.'s Toronto manager, said money was so hard to find for any kind of investment the hike would probably not be effective.
He said mortgage money from conventional or private sources-usually trust and insurance companies-was already running between 72 and 82 per cent.
Reg Ryan, vice-president of Mortgage Insurance Company of Canada, said other investment areas- such as bonds-were too attractive for an increase in N.H.A. lending to occur soon. He said there is very little of this government-insured money being turned into mortgages in Metro.
M.I.C.C.'s Ryan said the demand for mortgage money is away ahead of supply and this means Canada is entering another painful, tight money period.
Harry Sadler, chief of Toronto Metro Home Builders Association, said this would likely mean higher house prices in the months ahead and a slowdown in building.
Builders are already predicting Canada will fall short of the 170,000 housing units expected by C.M.H.C. in the 12-month period which began June 1.
Donald Kirkup, research director of the Toronto Real Estate Board, blamed mortgage companies for contributing to tight money by holding back funds in anticipation of the N.H.A. increase.
There is one consolation though. It should mean some more money for mortgages but we fear there won't be as many takers because of the increase.
He said it was "sad news" for young families just starting out.
Kirkup said the average price of a new house in Metro is close to $30,000, up about $5,500 in one year and resales around $24,000, up over $2,000.

We have a housing crisis in Canada and we have a slowdown in housing starts. We have the minister attempting to solve this problem by increasing the interest rate. We in the N.D.P. feel that this is not a proper solution, but that the solution should be to set up a federal ministry of housing and urban affairs, and to fix the rate of interest on N.H.A. mortgages at no more than 5 per cent. I regret, as does the minister and the government, that interest rates are as high as they are, but I think the hon. member should reflect upon the reasons. These rates are not high because of arbitrary action, but as a result of a shortage of money and a severe demand on this continent for money. I am sure the hon. member is also aware that the federal money available through C.M.H.C. is greater than it ever has been, but that the demand has been increased sharply. Finally, I am sure he is aware that as a result of recent revisions to the Bank Act, money is not available for housing from the chartered banks.
The government is doing everything it can to increase available money, but the interest rates reflect the economic condition of tight money supply. This is prevalent throughout the western world, together with a shortage of capital. The situation results from an over employment of monetary resources and an excessive demand for the same resources.
